description: The physical and link layers in depth: how bits become signals, survive noise and bandwidth limits, share a medium, and arrive without error. Taught to the depth of a leading digital communication systems course.
modelledOn: Proakis and Salehi, Fundamentals of Communication Systems
outcomes: Describe signals in time and frequency, compute bandwidth, and apply the Nyquist and Shannon limits to a channel.
Explain and simulate line codes and analog and digital modulation schemes and their trade-offs.
Design multiplexing schemes (FDM, TDM, WDM, CDM) for a given set of channels.
Compute and implement error detection and correction codes and evaluate their power.
Analyse flow-control protocols and compare circuit, packet and message switching.
Choose a transmission medium for a link given distance, bandwidth, cost and environment.

units.title: Data communication fundamentals
topics: Components of a communication system: source, transmitter, channel, receiver, destination
Simplex, half-duplex, full-duplex; serial and parallel; synchronous and asynchronous
Protocols and standards bodies: ITU-T, IEEE, IETF, ISO
Where this course sits: physical and data-link layers of the OSI model

units.title: Signals, bandwidth and noise
topics: Analog and digital signals; periodic signals; amplitude, frequency, phase, wavelength
Time and frequency domains; Fourier series and the spectrum of a square wave; composite signals
Bandwidth of a signal and of a channel; baseband and passband
Transmission impairments: attenuation, distortion, noise (thermal, crosstalk, impulse); decibels and SNR
Nyquist bit rate and Shannon capacity; computing the capacity of a telephone line and a Wi-Fi channel
Throughput, latency, jitter and bandwidth-delay product

units.title: Analog and digital transmission
topics: Digital-to-digital, analog-to-digital, digital-to-analog and analog-to-analog conversion as a map
Sampling theorem, quantisation, PCM and delta modulation; voice at 64 kbit/s
Transmission modes: parallel, serial asynchronous, serial synchronous, isochronous
Baud rate versus bit rate; signal element versus data element

units.title: Line coding and modulation
topics: Line coding requirements: DC balance, clock recovery, bandwidth; NRZ, NRZ-I, Manchester, differential Manchester, AMI, 4B/5B, 8B/10B
Block coding and scrambling
Digital-to-analog modulation: ASK, FSK, PSK, QPSK, QAM; constellation diagrams; bits per symbol
Analog modulation: AM, FM, PM and radio broadcasting
Simulating modulation and demodulation in software and observing the effect of noise

units.title: Multiplexing and spreading
topics: Frequency-division multiplexing; guard bands; radio and cable TV
Wavelength-division multiplexing in fibre
Time-division multiplexing: synchronous and statistical; T1/E1 framing
Code-division multiplexing and orthogonal codes
Spread spectrum: frequency hopping and direct sequence

units.title: Transmission media
topics: Guided media: twisted pair, coaxial, optical fibre; construction, bandwidth, attenuation, cost
Unguided media: radio, microwave, satellite, infrared; propagation modes and antennas
Comparing media for a rural school link: fibre, point-to-point wireless, satellite, 4G
Connectors and interfaces: RS-232, USB, RJ-45, SC/LC fibre

units.title: Error detection and correction
topics: Types of errors; redundancy; Hamming distance and the detection and correction bounds
Simple and two-dimensional parity; checksums and the Internet checksum
Cyclic codes and CRC: generator polynomials, division in hardware with shift registers, standard CRCs
Hamming codes and burst-error handling with interleaving
Introduction to convolutional and Reed-Solomon codes as used in mobile and storage

units.title: Data link control and flow control
topics: Framing: character count, byte stuffing, bit stuffing
Flow control: stop-and-wait, sliding window; efficiency and link utilisation
Error control with ARQ: stop-and-wait ARQ, go-back-N, selective repeat; sequence numbers
HDLC and PPP frame formats
Media access: ALOHA, CSMA, CSMA/CD, CSMA/CA; token passing; channelisation

units.title: Switching
topics: Circuit switching: space and time division switches; the telephone network
Packet switching: datagram and virtual circuit; store-and-forward delay
Message switching; comparison of delay, setup and reliability
Structure of a switch and a router; from switching to networking

schedule.title: Communication systems and standards
schedule.exercise: Draw the five components of a communication system for a mobile money SMS from sender to recipient, and name the standard body behind each interface.

tasks.title: Build a two-host link and label the source, transmitter, channel, receiver and destination, then send one packet and trace it
Configure a link in simplex, half-duplex and full-duplex modes, send traffic both ways and record which modes allow simultaneous transfer
Decide which standards body governs six given technologies and rank the effects on a local ISP in a short case scenario

schedule.title: Signals, spectrum and bandwidth
schedule.exercise: Sketch a square wave and its first five harmonics by hand, then estimate the bandwidth needed to carry it with acceptable shape.

tasks.title: Plot a sine wave and read off its amplitude, frequency and phase, then change each parameter and describe the effect on the plot
Sum the first 1, 3, 5 and 15 odd harmonics to build a square wave, plot each approximation and its spectrum, and compare the errors
Pass a composite signal through a low-pass filter of varying bandwidth and find the smallest bandwidth that keeps all bits recoverable

schedule.title: Impairments, capacity and performance
schedule.exercise: Compute the Shannon capacity of a telephone line and a Wi-Fi channel from given bandwidth and SNR, and say which limit applies to each.

tasks.title: Convert five attenuation and gain values to and from decibels and compute the SNR of a signal with added noise
Compute the Nyquist and Shannon rates for a 3 kHz line at 30 dB SNR and plot capacity against SNR to find the dominating limit
Measure latency, jitter and throughput on a simulated satellite link and compute its bandwidth-delay product to size a window for full utilisation

schedule.title: Conversion, sampling and transmission modes
schedule.exercise: Explain in a paragraph why telephone voice is sampled at 8000 samples per second and how that leads to 64 kbit/s.

tasks.title: Place eight given signal conversions into the four categories of digital-to-digital, analog-to-digital, digital-to-analog and analog-to-analog
Sample a 1 kHz tone at three rates, quantise to 3 bits, and plot each reconstruction to show aliasing and quantisation error
Compute bit rate, baud rate and data elements per signal element for four given schemes and find the scheme needing the least bandwidth

schedule.title: Line coding and digital modulation
schedule.exercise: Encode a short ASCII word in five line codes by hand and compare their DC balance and clock recovery properties.

tasks.title: Encode the bits 10110010 in NRZ, Manchester and AMI and plot each waveform, marking where clock recovery is possible
Draw the ASK, FSK and PSK waveforms for an 8-bit message, then plot QPSK and 16-QAM constellations and compute bits per symbol
Design a scrambling rule that avoids long runs of zeros in a bit stream, test it on a 64-bit string and prove the receiver recovers the original

schedule.title: Analog modulation and noise simulation
schedule.exercise: Explain why FM radio sounds clearer than AM in a thunderstorm, using the idea that noise changes amplitude more than frequency.

tasks.title: Generate an AM signal from a 1 kHz message on a 20 kHz carrier, plot it and compute its modulation index and bandwidth
Modulate and demodulate a bit stream with BPSK, add noise at five levels and plot the bit error rate against SNR
Compare BPSK and QPSK bit error rates at a fixed noise level and find the SNR at which each reaches an error rate below one in a thousand

schedule.title: Multiplexing and spread spectrum
schedule.exercise: Draw a frequency plan for 10 radio channels with guard bands inside a 1 MHz band and compute the guard band you can afford.

tasks.title: Place four voice channels of 4 kHz with 1 kHz guard bands on a spectrum plot and compute the total bandwidth required
Build a synchronous TDM frame for four 64 kbit/s channels, interleave their bytes, and compute the frame rate and line rate
Encode three users' bits with orthogonal Walsh codes, add the signals together and decode each user, then show what happens when codes are not orthogonal

schedule.title: Transmission media
schedule.exercise: Write a short recommendation for connecting a rural school to the Internet, comparing four media on cost, bandwidth and maintenance.

tasks.title: Compute the attenuation in decibels over 100 m for twisted pair, coaxial cable and fibre from given dB per km figures
Estimate the line-of-sight range and free-space loss for a 5 GHz point-to-point link between two towers 12 km apart
Build a school network with a wireless point-to-point backhaul, test throughput and delay, then compare it with a satellite link under the same load

schedule.title: Error detection
schedule.exercise: Compute the Hamming distance between several pairs of codewords and state how many errors a code of that distance detects and corrects.

tasks.title: Find the minimum Hamming distance of a small code of eight codewords and state how many errors it can detect and correct
Compute the Internet checksum for a 20-byte message and show a received message with a corrupted byte that the checksum fails to catch
Divide a 16-bit message by a generator polynomial to find its CRC, then flip each bit in turn and check which errors the CRC catches

schedule.title: Error correction
schedule.exercise: Explain why interleaving helps against burst errors in mobile networks, using a small grid example.

tasks.title: Encode four data bits with a Hamming(7,4) code, flip one bit and use the syndrome to locate and correct it
Interleave four Hamming codewords, apply a burst of three errors and show that deinterleaving turns it into single-bit errors that can be corrected
Compare the overhead and correcting power of a Hamming code, a repetition code and a Reed-Solomon code for a 1 percent error channel

schedule.title: Framing, flow control and ARQ
schedule.exercise: Compute the link utilisation of stop-and-wait for a 10 Mbit/s link with 20 ms delay and compare it to a sliding window.

tasks.title: Apply bit stuffing to a given bit stream containing the flag pattern and then remove the stuffing to recover the original data
Measure link utilisation of stop-and-wait against sliding window on a high-delay link, and choose the window size that fills the pipe
Run go-back-N and selective repeat on a lossy link at 5 percent loss, then compare retransmissions and throughput in a table

schedule.title: Data link protocols and media access
schedule.exercise: Write a short comparison of CSMA/CD and CSMA/CA, explaining why wireless networks cannot use collision detection.

tasks.title: Decode the fields of a given HDLC frame, including flag, address, control and checksum, and identify its frame type
Simulate ALOHA and slotted ALOHA with increasing load and plot throughput to find each peak, then compare with the theory
Simulate a shared medium of 10 stations under CSMA/CA with several contention window sizes and choose the setting that maximises throughput

schedule.title: Switching and the road to networking
schedule.exercise: Compute the end-to-end delay of sending a 1 MB file over three store-and-forward hops and compare it with a circuit-switched call.

tasks.title: Design a two-stage space-division switch for 16 inputs and count its crosspoints against a single crossbar
Send packets through a three-router datagram network, then use virtual circuits, and compare the paths and delay in each case
Build a network with two switches and a router, trace one packet through each device and explain which layer each device operates at
